prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, which brought the measurement of time to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18.

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean, original invention: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid interrogating many atoms at once, and Ye's group turned that into the most accurate measurements ever made, with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and, increasingly, many-body clock physics. It is confirmed by independent laboratories in several species and compared across continents, and its consequences are concrete: a redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and sharp tests of fundamental constants. Five colleagues placed it first or second, and I now judge that consensus to rest on substance rather than on mere opening momentum. The two-name credit is unusually clean, and the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover adjacent but different steps.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is category: some will read this as extraordinary metrology and instrumentation rather than a discovery of new physics, and the precursors in ion clocks and frequency combs, together with other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat) are not in the credited names. Two clock-related prizes in 2005 and 2012 might also lead someone to argue that atomic precision measurement is already well served. My own view is that the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct conceptual step, but I accept that this is a judgment, not a fact.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a clear invention with overwhelming confirmation, while noting that Nobel recognition of instrumentation needs a precedent and that Krivanek's STEM corrector work sits outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that B017 is mature and that the invention is real, but her own caveat is where I land. The credited trio leaves a known gap in the scanning-transmission lineage, and the prize case rests on enabling imaging rather than a new physical result. I put B009 ahead because the lattice clock pairs the same kind of enabling measurement with a physical-principle step (the magic wavelength) and with immediate fundamental-physics reach, so it is easier to defend as a discovery-class invention. I would not object to B017 reaching the final stage, but I do not rank it above B009.

responses.point: Pearce puts B052 first and argues that the decisive IceCube pair is Halzen and Karle, with Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage complicating a fair three-person split; he also treats source identification as still partial.
responses.response: IceCube is outside my own field and I defer to him and to Danielsson on the instrument history. I do take his attribution point seriously: if the committee cannot defend a three-name split, that is a real weakness compared with the Katori and Ye pairing, which no one has disputed. On maturity I accept that the diffuse flux is established, but a prize anchored on that discovery while source identification is moderate-significance invites the question of what is being rewarded. I would want that settled before choosing B052 over B009, and I see it as a close and legitimate competitor rather than a weaker one.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first as measurement physics whose reach is set by what can be measured, credits Katori with the founding idea and Ye with the record accuracy, and discloses that Ye trained in John Hall's laboratory where he himself spent a research period.
responses.response: I largely agree with his reading of the attribution and with the weighting of Katori's founding idea against Ye's realisation. I would qualify one point: because Ye's link to Hall is the source of his disclosed connection, the committee should record that tie but treat it as a lineage fact, not a reason to discount Ye's independent contribution to the 1e-18 milestones. I also think the case is strengthened, not weakened, by the fact that several colleagues with no connection to that lineage reach the same ranking.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics first as a conceptually clean, uncontested method with four decades of use, while worrying it may be read as chemistry after the 1998 prize.
responses.response: His attribution argument is the best of any candidate: one paper, two names, no dispute. I disagree only mildly on priority. The 1998 chemistry prize is a genuine overlap risk, and I think the committee should be honest that B041 would sit on the physics-chemistry boundary. Where I qualify his case is on novelty of the physical result: it is a computational technique that other fields use more than physics proper does, whereas the lattice clock changes what physics experiments can measure. I think B041 deserves discussion, but it is not a reason to move B009 down.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B009 first, notes that B008 is conceptually distinct from the 2025 macroscopic-tunnelling work but warns that a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon may look unbalanced, and flags Wallraff, Nakamura and Devoret's overlapping role.
responses.response: I opened with B008 and I now move away from it. His distinction between circuit QED and the 2025 discovery is correct scientifically, but the sequencing and the missing credit for Wallraff are real problems, and Eriksson and Lindroth raise the same timing worry. Because this is my own field, I do not want my enthusiasm to be mistaken for balance across physics. I keep B008 as an alternative rather than a preference and ask the committee to weigh it without relying on my advocacy.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards an optical lattice clock as a physics discovery or as precision instrumentation.
Whether Katori and Ye alone adequately represent a field where Sr, Yb and Hg groups at several national laboratories reached 1e-18.
Whether the 2025 circuit prize should depress B008 relative to B014 or B009 in a final ordering, given my own proximity to it.
Whether the atom-physics share in the last two decades (2005, 2012, and possibly now) leaves a balanced spread of fields.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT at Chalmers and work on superconducting circuits, so B008 (circuit QED) is in my own research field and I would recuse on any decision that turns on it. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum are documented links to the circuit field, and Chalmers hosted researchers tied to the 2025 prize. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye (B009), or the other candidates is apparent from my provided profile.
